newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac doubts Italy can make first EMU group.
newsitem.headline: Chirac doubts Italy can make first EMU group.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac cast doubt on Tuesday on whether Italy would be among the first group of European Union countries to join a single currency in 1999.
Chirac told businessmen during a tour of northern France:

"Things are going to go pretty quickly now...for some countries which have made the effort to clean up their economic and financial situation...It may take a little bit longer for those who are further behind, like Italy."
His remarks drew a swift response from Italy which accused him of meddling in Rome's affairs.
"We cannot but view (them) as grave, grave because our country has made an exceptional effort to enter Europe," Italian Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni told reporters.
"Chirac has every right to look at the state of his own country, without interfering in the internal choices of a country which is putting together a budget," he added.
"We don't pass judgment on what others do and we expect others to act the same way."
The row sets up a possible clash at this week's Franco-Italian summit, starting in Naples on Thursday night.

Shortly before Chirac spoke, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi had told reporters in Rome that some partners, including France and Germany, were motivated by fear of competition from dynamic Italian industry,

Speaking in a depressed textile region, Chirac said France had suffered from devaluations of the Italian lira, the British pound and the Spanish peseta, which had hit its textile industry harder than southeast Asian imports.
"(It is) quite obvious that the lira's movement is completely incompatible with a single European market, even if it has rebounded slightly recently," Chirac said.
A fixed link between the euro and the currencies of non-founder members of the European unit was an "unavoidable" necessity, he added.
Chirac's comments could also heighten a sense in Italy that some European states, including economic powerhouse Germany, are actively trying to bar Italy from being a founder of the euro.
Italian Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said earlier that some European states had speeded up their efforts to try to keep Italy out.

Visco told a news conference that the government had changed its approach to the budget earlier this month. He said that was because of "an acceleration towards convergence in some countries linked not only to the conviction but also to the hope and desire that our country would be excluded." He would not name the countries.
Italy unveiled a tougher-than-expected 1997 budget last week to try to meet the economic criteria in the Maastricht treaty for joining a single currency when it is launched.

Prodi, whose budget package has sparked criticism from opposition and business leaders, denied he recently tried to convince his Spanish counterpart Jose Maria Aznar to try to persade EU partners to modify some criteria.
Spain has also accelerated its push to join the single currency and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar reaffirmed his country's commitment to being among the first wave.

"We will be there," Aznar told the Financial Times in an interview published on Monday. "I am ready to take whatever measures are necessary to succeed, because I am absolutely persuaded that Spain is staking its stability and prosperity in this bet."
